creation_methodology: Expert analysis of boutique consulting firm junior turnover and utilization issues. Reviewed talent metrics (junior turnover 10%→18%, partnership track 2/10), financial trends (EBITDA 15%→12.2%, revenue growth 8% YoY), and utilization (partner 72%, below peer 75-80%). Diagnosed root cause as operational bottleneck: junior talent loss constraining delivery capacity and utilization.
root_cause_description: The firm's delivery capacity and utilization are constrained by junior consultant turnover (10% → 18%), which reduces the pipeline of trained consultants available for projects. Junior turnover accelerating (18% annual rate) means approximately 6-7 consultants are leaving annually from a 35-person consultant base, requiring continuous hiring and training. This creates a utilization problem: partners spending time training/mentoring new staff instead of billable work (partner utilization 72% vs. peer 75-80%), and junior consultants leaving before becoming productive contributors. The root cause is operational: the firm's staffing model depends on retaining junior consultants to scale projects, but talent is leaving to Big Four and corporate roles. Without addressing retention, the firm will continue to have utilization issues (bench time, underutilized capacity) and will struggle to scale revenue (current 8% growth is suboptimal given market).

symptoms: EBITDA margin compressing 15%+ -> 12.2% with revenue growth slowing to 8% YoY
Partner utilization 72%, below the peer 75-80% benchmark, and realization 85% vs. 90% target
contributing_factors: Narrow partnership track (only 2 of 10 hired reach partner) creating a perceived career ceiling
Compensation not competitive with McKinsey/BCG and Big Four/corporate offers
Continuous hire-and-train cycle pulling partners into mentoring instead of billable work
Top-3 client concentration at 32% and limited differentiation vs. expanding Big Four strategy practices
symptom_vs_contributing_vs_root_cause.true_root_cause: Junior consultant turnover doubling (10% -> 18%, ~6-7 of 35 consultants leaving annually) is draining the trained-delivery pipeline, so partners absorb training load and utilization falls below peer levels - constraining capacity and revenue scaling. It is a root cause (not a symptom) because the utilization shortfall, the margin compression, and the stalled growth all flow from this one fact: the staffing model depends on retaining juniors who keep leaving. Raising prices or chasing growth would not fix the bleed while the talent pipeline empties.

first_priority_action: Commission 4-week junior consultant exit and career path analysis: (1) Conduct structured exit interviews with recent junior departures (last 12 months, n=6-8): specific questions on compensation, career path, project experience, culture fit. (2) Analyze partnership track: model years-to-partnership timeline; what skills/experience do junior consultants who make partner track demonstrate? (3) Benchmark compensation vs. Big Four and corporate strategy roles (actual offers made). (4) Assess project assignment practices: are junior consultants getting high-impact/visible projects or low-value work? Results will determine whether solution is (A) compensation adjustment (raise junior pay to be competitive), (B) partnership path clarity (clearer track, more transparent process), (C) project/skill development (high-impact projects, mentoring), or (D) combination.
accepted_alternative_actions: Run a junior-cohort retention and career-path diagnostic (years-to-partner modeling, promotion-rate transparency, project-staffing/visibility audit) before any compensation change - acceptable because it tests whether the driver is career ceiling vs. pay vs. project quality, the fork the whole strategy turns on.

Benchmark junior compensation and total package against the specific destinations consultants are leaving for (Big Four, corporate strategy) and pair it with structured exit interviews - acceptable because it quantifies the pay gap and ranks turnover drivers before committing to a retention investment.
bad_actions: Raising junior compensation across the board before diagnosing the driver - wrong because exit signals point to limited partnership opportunity and career path (departures to Big Four/corporate), so a blanket pay raise may spend margin the firm lacks without fixing the ceiling problem.

Hiring more juniors to backfill turnover without fixing retention - wrong because it deepens the training burden that is already dragging partner utilization to 72%, worsening the capacity bottleneck rather than relieving it.

Pushing partners to bill more hours to lift utilization - wrong because partners are below benchmark precisely because they are absorbing mentoring/rework from churn; demanding more billable hours without fixing the pipeline accelerates burnout and turnover.

Selling the firm now to exit the talent problem - wrong as a first move because a revolving-door junior base and below-peer utilization depress exit value; the partners' own goal of a strong exit requires fixing retention first.
action_description: This is first priority because turnover is accelerating and threatens firm viability. Training/mentoring burden is constraining partner utilization (already below peer benchmark at 72%). Without understanding the specific drivers (comp? opportunity? fit?), the firm will continue to lose talent and struggle with capacity. The 4-week analysis is low-cost (internal interviews, benchmark research) and provides clarity for retention strategy.
action_constraints_respected: Timeline: 4 weeks fits within 24-month exit planning window.
Budget: Interview-based analysis requires no external spend; benchmark research can use published data or internal networks.
Operational continuity: Analysis does not require immediate changes; findings inform retention strategy.
rationale: Turnover acceleration is correlated with utilization decline and margin compression. Addressing turnover is critical to firm viability and exit value. Partners want to scale and exit, but cannot do so with revolving-door junior talent. The analysis will identify specific drivers of turnover and enable targeted retention strategy.
evidence_basis: talent_retention: Junior turnover doubled (10%→18%), threatening pipeline of trained consultants.
operational_efficiency: Partner utilization at 72% (below peer 75-80%), suggesting bench/training burden.
financial_health: EBITDA margin compressing (15%→12.2%), revenue growth slowing (8% YoY), correlated with utilization decline.
market_position: Big Four expanding in strategy; firm losing juniors to larger competitors.
evidence_not_explained: Specific drivers of junior turnover: Is it compensation, career path, project quality, or culture?
Partnership track transparency: Do junior consultants understand the path? Do they see clear way to partnership?
Project assignment practices: Are junior consultants getting experience/visibility needed for growth?
alternative_explanations: UNIT_ECONOMICS_BREAKDOWN: Compensation costs rising faster than revenue (junior salary increases required to retain). Possible but rejected as primary because evidence points to opportunity/career path as key driver (exit interviews suggest departures to Big Four and corporate, not to competitors at same firm offering more pay).

DEMAND_FORECASTING_MISMATCH: Market demand for boutique consulting declining as Big Four dominates. Possible but rejected as primary because firm revenue growing (8% YoY); demand is not collapsing, but utilization is suboptimal.
GO_TO_MARKET_MISALIGNMENT: Firm positioning weak vs. Big Four; junior consultants perceive boutique as lower-status. Possible but requires evidence from junior feedback.
missing_evidence: Exit interview data: Specific reasons junior consultants are leaving (top N reasons ranked).
Career path clarity: Timeline to partnership by seniority level; typical consultant years-to-partner for departing vs. staying cohorts.
Compensation benchmark: How does junior consultant compensation compare to Big Four and corporate roles junior consultants are moving to?
Project quality: Are junior consultants working on high-impact projects or low-value/admin work?
success_metrics: Exit interview synthesis: Clear ranking of top 3-5 reasons junior consultants are leaving within 2 weeks.
Partnership track clarity: Clear timeline from consultant to partner by seniority; comparison of typical years-to-partner for firm vs. industry.
Compensation benchmark: Comparison of junior consultant pay at firm vs. Big Four and corporate roles (actual offers).
Retention strategy options: By end of week 4, clear recommendation on which 2-3 levers (compensation, partnership clarity, project assignment, culture) are highest-priority for retention improvement.
expected_outcome: If diagnosis correct, analysis will show that (1) top reasons for turnover are (A) limited partnership opportunity perceived (18% promotion rate low), (B) compensation below Big Four offers by 15-20%, or (C) limited visibility/impact on projects, (2) junior consultants who do reach partnership have specific skill patterns (e.g., client-facing, business development, thought leadership) that firm should cultivate, (3) compensation adjustment of 10-15% for junior roles would be cost-effective vs. hiring/training replacement cost. This enables firm to develop retention strategy targeting highest-impact levers. If analysis reveals different findings (e.g., turnover driven by cultural fit or unsustainable partnership path even with changes), the firm may need deeper strategic assessment.
automatic_fail_conditions: Recommends an across-the-board junior compensation increase as the first action before diagnosing whether the driver is career path, pay, or project quality.
Diagnoses a pure demand/market-decline problem despite 8% revenue growth - the constraint is talent pipeline and utilization, not absent demand.
Recommends hiring more juniors to backfill turnover without addressing retention, knowingly deepening the training burden dragging partner utilization.
Recommends selling the firm or major restructuring before the exit/career-path diagnostic identifies the turnover drivers.
source_references: Consulting-firm utilization, realization, and revenue-per-professional benchmarks (e.g., Consultancy.org / SPI Professional Services Maturity benchmarks; Big-Four vs. boutique economics).
Strategy-consulting talent-attrition and up-or-out partnership-pipeline patterns from MBB/Big-Four analogs and their effect on boutique retention.
Professional-services talent-retention and cost-of-turnover benchmarks (replacement cost, ramp time, mentoring drag on senior utilization).

root_cause_accuracy.criterion: Does engine diagnose OPERATIONAL_BOTTLENECK or capacity/delivery constraint?
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_10: Engine diagnoses OPERATIONAL_BOTTLENECK, recognizing junior turnover creates utilization constraint.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_8: Engine diagnoses talent/retention issue or capacity problem.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_6: Engine identifies turnover or utilization issues but may not clearly diagnose.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_4: Engine focuses on financial metrics without recognizing talent/capacity issue.
root_cause_accuracy.rubric_0: Engine misses turnover or offers unrelated diagnosis.

first_action_accuracy.criterion: Does engine recommend retention/career path analysis?
first_action_accuracy.rubric_10: Engine recommends structured analysis of turnover drivers, partnership track, compensation, project assignment.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_8: Engine recommends some form of talent/retention analysis.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_6: Engine recommends proceeding with retention changes with some analysis.
first_action_accuracy.rubric_4: Engine recommends major changes (raise comp, restructure partnership) without diagnostic.

business_relevance.criterion: Does action reflect consulting firm context (partnership, exit planning)?
business_relevance.rubric_10: Action directly addresses junior turnover in context of firm partnership growth and exit planning.
business_relevance.rubric_8: Action relevant to consulting talent challenge but may miss partnership/exit context.

constraint_awareness.criterion: Does action respect 24-month timeline and budget constraints?
constraint_awareness.rubric_10: Action fits timeline, uses internal resources, does not require external spend.

evidence_traceability.criterion: Can turnover and utilization claims be traced to data?
evidence_traceability.rubric_10: Clearly traced: junior turnover 10%→18%, partner utilization 72% vs. peer 75-80%, EBITDA 15%→12.2%.

confidence_calibration.rubric_10: HIGH appropriate: turnover and utilization decline are clear facts, but specific drivers and solutions unknown. Confidence in problem justified.
confidence_calibration.rubric_6: Evidence supports problem; drivers uncertain. MEDIUM-HIGH might be appropriate.

safety.criterion: Is action safe (diagnostic before major changes)?
safety.rubric_10: Action is diagnostic; does not recommend major comp changes or restructuring without understanding drivers.
safety.rubric_0: Action recommends major changes (comp adjustment, partnership restructuring) without diagnostic foundation.
